lesson.title: AC Coupling: Filtering Out the Baseline to See the Ripple
lesson.summary: AC coupling inserts a capacitor in series with the oscilloscope's input so any steady DC level is blocked and only the changing, AC part of the signal reaches the display, which is invaluable for viewing a small ripple riding on top of a large DC voltage.
lesson.body:
Every oscilloscope input offers a coupling choice, and one of the two options is AC coupling. Selecting it places a capacitor in series between the probe tip and the rest of the scope's input circuitry. A capacitor, as you already know, does not pass a steady DC current once it has charged up, so any constant offset in the signal you are probing gets blocked before it ever reaches the vertical amplifier. Only the parts of the signal that are actually changing, the AC component, make it through and get displayed.

The reason this is useful becomes obvious with a concrete situation. Imagine you are probing the output of a DC power supply that is supposed to hold a steady 12 volts, but you suspect it has a small amount of ripple riding on top of that level, perhaps 50 millivolts of leftover hum at the line frequency. If you tried to view this in DC coupled mode at a vertical sensitivity fine enough to actually resolve 50 millivolts of detail, the entire 12 volt DC level would run the trace off the top of the screen instantly, since even a modest few volts per division setting puts 12 volts many divisions above the display's edge. AC coupling solves this by removing the 12 volt baseline entirely, letting the trace sit near the center of the screen so you can turn the vertical sensitivity down to a fine setting and watch just the 50 millivolt wiggle in detail.

Under the hood, the series capacitor and the scope's own input resistance, typically 1 megohm, form a simple high pass filter, exactly the kind of RC filter built from a capacitor and a resistor that you have already studied. Its cutoff frequency is given by the familiar relationship f-c equals 1 divided by 2 pi R C. As an illustration, if a scope used a coupling capacitor of 0.1 microfarads in series with its 1 megohm input resistance, the cutoff frequency would be f-c equals 1 over 2 times pi times 1,000,000 ohms times 0.0000001 farads, which works out to roughly 1.6 hertz. Frequencies well above that pass through essentially unattenuated, while true DC, at zero hertz, is blocked completely, and anything very close to that cutoff gets partially attenuated and shifted in phase, which is why AC coupling is not appropriate for measuring signals near or below that cutoff frequency.

The trade off is exactly what that filtering behavior implies: AC coupling throws away all information about the actual DC level of the signal. You can see that the ripple exists and measure its size, but you cannot tell from an AC coupled trace whether the underlying DC rail is really sitting at 12 volts, 11 volts, or 13 volts, because the capacitor has erased that information before it reached the display. Knowing when that trade off is worth making, and when it is not, is exactly the question the next chapter takes up.
